_meta.what_this_is: What a unit has to cost to win each kind of buyer, and which counterparties have a structural reason to buy. Every number restates a cited row on the Costs or Deals tabs; rows marked derived are arithmetic on those inputs with the formula printed.
_meta.method: Built 2026-09-02 from the site's own benchmarks, cost bands, tracker and site records, with the fixed-staffing inputs read from Idaho National Laboratory's cached cost reports. No new sources were fetched; the open questions each row ends with are the next research pass. Findings from the 2026-09-02 pass (data/research/2026-09-02-prospects) are copied in by tools/merge_answers.py; the hand-written rows above them were updated by hand after reading each finding.
_meta.derived_note: Derived figures are conversions of cited inputs at stated assumptions, not estimates of what any reactor will cost. Change the assumption and the number moves; the formula is printed so a reader can.

conversion.question: How much price does each $1,000/kWe cost?
conversion.formula: $/MWh per $1,000/kWe = 1,000 × CRF ÷ (8.76 × capacity factor); CRF = r(1+r)^n ÷ ((1+r)^n − 1)
conversion.note: A rule of thumb for reading the segments below: at a 5% real discount rate over 20 years and a 95% capacity factor, every $1,000/kWe of capital adds about $10/MWh to the price. Over 40 years it is about $7. The rate and the 20-year life are the University of Michigan study's; the 95% capacity factor is INL's and NEI's. It is a conversion, not a cost estimate, and it leaves out fuel, staff and financing during construction.

segments.name: Rural Alaska and Nunavut community grids
segments.incumbent: Diesel cost of service certified by the regulator at $410–1,950/MWh across rural Alaska; Nunavut's territorial utility charges $555–1,130/MWh by customer class.
segments.price_form: Utility rate base or a subsidised tariff. Commercial and industrial load in Alaska pays the full unsubsidised cost, so it is the customer to price against.
segments.term: Rate-based, so no fixed term; the state's PCE program is the settlement mechanism.
segments.verdict: Every published microreactor estimate beats this incumbent. Price is not the constraint.
segments.blocker: Load. Single villages draw tens of kilowatts, twenty times too small for a 1 MWe unit; only hub communities like Kotzebue at 19.7 GWh a year, or an aggregated tribal utility, present a load a reactor can serve. Nunavut adds sealift logistics and the absence of a Canadian microreactor licence.
segments.first_deal: A mid-size hub at $600–1,000/MWh, owned by the utility or a tribal power company inside the rate base, with public capital: the federal government already pays about $5,000/kW for non-diesel capacity in a 170-person village.

segments.name: Off-grid mines and mineral processing
segments.incumbent: Industrial self-generation in the Canadian North at $250–600/MWh, with a tail to $1,200. Natural Resources Canada puts a first-of-a-kind 20 MWe unit for mining at C$200–350M and expects a 20–60% cost advantage over diesel. Last Energy's 20 MWe unit was reported in 2023 at project costs below $100 million, about $5,000/kWe.
segments.price_form: Fixed $/kWh below the incumbent diesel cost, developer-owned behind the fence; 15-year terms at Kathleen Valley and Essakane, 16 at Syama. Mid-tier miners also build and own their own plants, so an owned unit has to be sellable too.
segments.term: 15–16 years is normal off-grid; mine life caps it.
segments.verdict: INL's first unit at $325/MWh sits inside the band and loses to cheap diesel at the bottom of it. The mass-produced unit at $120–150/MWh beats the whole band.
segments.blocker: Mine life against payback: Diavik's solar arrived with two years of production left, and Red Dog closes around 2032. Fleet electrification moves a 25 MW mine to 35–40 MW. And the northern operator's stated fear is a grid collapse at minus 40, so the reactor has to prove it firms the microgrid.
segments.first_deal: A new long-life mine, or a relocatable 20 MWe unit that can move to the next site, sold through the off-grid power contractor that already holds the site contract.

segments.name: Hospitals, water utilities and civic anchors
segments.incumbent: A Southern California clinic buys behind-the-meter power at 15 cents/kWh, flat for 30 years, with no host capital; sub-acute care facilities pay 22–25 cents with a 2% escalator. segments.incumbent: Wholesale colocation asks $196.25 per kW a month, about $269/MWh drawn continuously, for firm delivered power with space and interconnection; PJM capacity clears at $333.44/MW-day, about $121,700 per MW-year before energy. findings.question: the primary source for Oklo's stated first-unit cost and its expected $/MWh, and the slide behind the DOE clean-firm band ($63-99 gas with carbon capture, $66-109 advanced nuclear, $69-119 renewables plus storage) that a reporter attributed to an Oklo shareholder presentation. findings.finding: Utility Dive attributes all three figures to Oklo's Q2 2024 disclosures: the $145 million first-powerhouse cost to CFO R. Craig Bealmear speaking on Oklo's Q2 2024 earnings call, and both the $40-90/MWh expected levelized cost and the DOE clean-firm band (gas with carbon capture $63-99/MWh, advanced nuclear $66-109/MWh, renewables plus storage $69-119/MWh) to 'its shareholder presentation.' That presentation is identifiable and public: Oklo filed its Q2 2024 Shareholder Letter as Exhibit 99.1 to an August 13, 2024 Form 8-K, a 26-slide deck. Reading the full text of all 26 slides (including the hidden screen-reader captions describing each slide's graphic content) and grep'ing the raw filing for '$63', '$66', '$69', '$99', '$109', '$119', 'MWh', 'carbon capture' and 'clean firm' turns up zero matches anywhere in the filing. The closest slide (12 of 26) is captioned 'Strategically cost-competitive and highly repeatable' and lists reactor sizes (15 MW, 50 MW, 100+ MW) but carries no cost or $/MWh figures. So for the $40-90/MWh figure and the DOE clean-firm band specifically, only the reporter's own reading could be verified; the primary slide Utility Dive describes was not found in Oklo's SEC-filed presentation. The $145 million figure rests on a spoken quote attributed to a named executive on an earnings call, which is a more solid (if still secondhand) attribution.

prospects.name: Doyon Utilities (Fort Wainwright and Fort Greely, Alaska)
prospects.load: Electric, heat, water and wastewater systems at Alaska Army installations; capacity not stated in the award record
prospects.documented: An Alaska Native corporation joint venture holds a 51-year utility privatisation worth up to $3.08B, with $895M obligated since 2007, roughly $60M a year, and its generation is coal and oil delivered by rail and barge. Fort Wainwright is one of the nine Janus candidate installations and the only one whose displaced fuel is priced at Alaskan rates; it has not been matched to a vendor. Fort Wainwright was not among the five installations matched to vendors on 2026-08-26. A 2011-2012 rate dispute shows the contract runs as cost-of-service regulation: Doyon claimed $79M of plant additions in its rate base and said it was losing $1.1M a month across three installations, and the additions were contested case by case.
prospects.fit: The reactor enters as an asset inside a rate base a regulator already approves, so it does not have to win a $/kW contest. The unit can be 5–20 MW because the plant it supplements is a central heat-and-power station.
prospects.sale_shape: Rate-based generation inside the existing 10 U.S.C. 2688 contract, with the delivered-fuel line as the saving the contractor already prices.
prospects.next_question: What does Doyon's current RCA revenue requirement imply per MWh at Fort Wainwright, and would DLA Energy accept a reactor as a plant addition under the 2688 contract, given how the $79M of additions was contested in 2012?

findings.question: What is Doyon's delivered cost of coal and oil per MWh at Fort Wainwright, and does the privatisation contract allow new generation to be added to the rate base?

The contract does operate as cost-of-service rate-base regulation: in a 2011-2012 dispute Doyon said it was losing $1.1 million a month at Fort Wainwright, Fort Greely and Fort Richardson combined, after claiming $79 million of plant additions in its rate base that the government called inaccurate, which shows the rate base does absorb new capital additions (Doyon separately added a 2 MW oil-fired generator at Fort Wainwright's coal plant in 2009) but that specific additions are contested case by case rather than automatically approved. Separately, Fort Wainwright was excluded from the Army's Janus program: the August 26, 2026 selection named five vendor-installation pairs (Fort Bragg, Fort Campbell, Fort Hood, Fort Benning, Fort Drum), and Fort Wainwright was not one of them, so it remains an unmatched Janus candidate as of this research.

prospects.name: Copper Valley Electric Association (Valdez and Glennallen)
prospects.load: An islanded cooperative serving about 3,800 members; two 15 MWt units studied to replace the Valdez cogeneration unit
prospects.documented: A completed pre-feasibility study found a micro modular reactor a match for the cooperative's needs, with cooperative ownership beating vendor ownership, year-round heat sales pivotal and federal tax credits worth 30–50% of capital. The board tabled the project indefinitely in August 2023, and the vendor, USNC, entered Chapter 11 in 2024. Alaska's SB 177 removed the legislative siting requirement in 2022. The board's own release says it tabled the project on economics: too much risk for the members to own and operate it, and the vendor could not make an owner-operator PPA pencil without additional year-round heat or power customers. The release leaves the door open, and names Westinghouse, Oklo, NuScale and Radiant as vendors the cooperative had already talked to.
prospects.fit: The study, the site (a bedrock bench near the Trans-Alaska Pipeline) and the state law are all done. What is missing is a vendor with a licensable 5–15 MWe unit and heat offtake.
prospects.sale_shape: Cooperative-owned unit in the rate base, with heat sold to a Valdez offtaker; the study says vendor ownership loses.
prospects.next_question: Which year-round heat or power customer in Valdez would make an owner-operator PPA pencil, and would the board re-open the study with one of the four vendors it already vetted?

findings.question: Why did the board table it: cost, vendor risk or something else in the cached release? And is the cooperative open to re-running the study with a different vendor?
findings.finding: CVEA's own account (the August 9, 2023 release, reprinted in Ruralite's September 2023 issue) says the board tabled the project on economics, not vendor risk: after the fall-2022 feasibility study, CVEA's internal economic analysis found the project technically feasible but concluded there was too much economic risk for the members to own and operate it themselves, so CVEA instead pursued a power purchase agreement with USNC as owner-operator. USNC then determined in July 2023 that a PPA meeting CVEA's needs would require additional year-round heat and/or power customers to be economically feasible, and without that PPA CVEA said it could no longer pursue the project. The release explicitly leaves the door open, stating the co-op will continue to monitor the technology and may reassess if economic conditions improve, and outgoing CEO Travis Million said the MMR technology may not be the solution today but could still be in the future. The same document shows CVEA was already vendor-agnostic before choosing USNC: it names Westinghouse, Oklo, NuScale and Radiant Technologies as other MMR manufacturers it was in conversations with, and picked USNC because the projected unit size best matched CVEA's system, not out of exclusivity. No CVEA statement since USNC's October 2024 Chapter 11 filing was found reacting to it or naming a prospective replacement vendor.

prospects.documented: The first SMR licence application in Canada, filed in 2019 with a licence to prepare site and a federal environmental assessment, was paused by the regulator in 2024 when the parent vendor filed for bankruptcy. Ontario Power Generation is a co-venturer and the regulator's page still reads paused. NANO Nuclear acquired Global First Power from USNC on 2025-10-22, for the assumption of about $640,000 owed to the CNSC, and says it now owns the licence application; the CNSC's own page, last modified 2026-01-15, still reads paused and names no new owner.

findings.question: Who owns the Global First Power venture after the bankruptcy sale, and will the CNSC application be transferred or withdrawn?
findings.finding: NANO Nuclear Energy Inc. (via its subsidiary Kronos MMR Inc.) now owns Global First Power Limited (GFPL). NANO's press release states it acquired GFPL from USNC on October 22, 2025, with 'the principal consideration paid' being NANO's assumption of 'an approximately $640,000 liability owed by GFPL to the CNSC,' and that NANO 'now directly owns the regulatory licensing application' to build a KRONOS MMR demonstration at Chalk River, continuing from GFPL's completed Vendor Design Review and submitted first part of the licence-to-prepare-site (LTPS) application. This is a separate transaction from Standard Nuclear's $28M stalking-horse purchase of USNC's fuel-related assets in the same Chapter 11 case. However, CNSC's own project page, last modified 2026-01-15 (three months after the GFPL deal closed), still states only that 'CNSC staff have paused all work related to the environmental assessment and the application review for the licence to prepare site as of August 2024' and attributes the pause to USNC's bankruptcy — it makes no mention of NANO Nuclear, Kronos MMR, or any transfer. So ownership has changed and NANO says it is continuing the project, but the CNSC docket itself has not yet been updated to reflect a transfer, reinstatement, or withdrawal.

prospects.name: Teck and NANA Regional Corporation, Red Dog mine
prospects.load: About 25 MW, off-grid and diesel-only, burning roughly 14.6 million gallons a year; an 8.8 MW solar farm is expected to deliver about 2 MW in summer
prospects.documented: The sharpest microreactor-shaped load in North America: one 20 MWe unit would replace the whole 24.5 MW diesel station. The landowner is an Alaska Native corporation, the power contractor is TUGLIQ, and the mine's closure is planned around 2032. Teck declined on the record to give a cost when asked about the solar project; the mine burns roughly 40,000 gallons of diesel a day, and the solar project's structure is TUGLIQ building and operating on land partly owned by NANA and selling the power to Teck under a negotiated PPA.
prospects.fit: A single 20 MWe unit matches the load exactly; only a relocatable unit fits the remaining mine life.
prospects.sale_shape: Third-party-owned generation behind the fence under a term contract, with the unit moving to the next site at closure.
prospects.next_question: Would NANA extend the land-and-PPA structure it gave TUGLIQ's solar project to a relocatable reactor, and what does 40,000 gallons a day come to per MWh at Teck's delivered price?

findings.question: What does Teck pay per delivered gallon and per MWh today, and would NANA, as landowner, take an ownership stake in a relocatable unit?
findings.finding: Neither figure is publicly disclosed: no $/gallon or $/MWh cost for Red Dog's diesel generation appears in any Teck filing, sustainability report or news account found, and a Teck spokesperson explicitly declined to give a cost estimate when reporters asked about the mine's planned solar project (reported March 2026). What is confirmed is scale and structure: Red Dog burns roughly 40,000 gallons of diesel each day, and the mine's plan to displace some of that diesel is a solar-plus-battery project that Tugliq Energy, a Canadian company, would build and operate, selling the power back to Teck under a negotiated power purchase agreement, on a 30-acre site partly on land owned by NANA. That build-own-operate-and-sell-power structure is the closest existing precedent for how a reactor deal at Red Dog would likely be structured. NANA's own 'Future of Red Dog Mine' page, which focuses entirely on permitting the Aktigiruq/Anarraaq extension before the current Aqqaluk ore deposit is exhausted, makes no mention of energy generation, ownership stakes in power assets, or nuclear technology, and no public NANA statement on taking an ownership position in generation of any kind was found anywhere.

prospects.name: Agnico Eagle and Nukik Corporation, Kivalliq region
prospects.load: The Meadowbank complex and Meliadine mine burn about 33.5 million litres of diesel a year, three-quarters of the 44.5 million litres the proposed line would displace
prospects.documented: The competing supply is a C$3.2B, 1,200 km transmission line from Manitoba, revised up from C$1.2B, that does not arrive until 2032. The line is Inuit-owned through Nukik and also serves five communities on Qulliq's territory-wide diesel fleet at $555–1,130/MWh. prospects.documented: A territorial Crown utility that publishes the number a developer needs: a regulated retail rate two to four times any published microreactor estimate, on a fleet that is entirely diesel. Nineteen of the territory's 25 diesel plants exceed 1 MW of installed capacity, Iqaluit at 13.6 MW, on a fleet of about 76 MW. findings.question: Which Nunavut communities draw more than 1 MW year-round, and has the territory taken a position on nuclear under its own energy strategy?
findings.finding: QEC's installed-capacity data, as tabulated by community on Wikipedia's list of Nunavut generating stations (the per-community figures are not fetched from a QEC page here), shows 19 of Nunavut's 25 diesel plants exceed 1 MW of installed capacity: Iqaluit leads at 13.6 MW, followed by Rankin Inlet (3.55 MW) and Cambridge Bay (3.11 MW), down to Sanikiluaq at 1.2 MW; only six communities (Chesterfield Inlet, Grise Fiord, Kimmirut, Kugaaruk, Naujaat, Whale Cove) sit below 1 MW. QEC's fleet totals approximately 76,000 kilowatts of installed diesel capacity across all 25 communities. On the nuclear question, QEC's own 2023-2026 Corporate Plan devotes a full section to alternative energy that discusses solar PV, battery storage, geothermal and district heating at length and does not mention nuclear power, small modular reactors, or microreactors anywhere; its stated constraint is that its small customer base and the cost of its generation projects limit its financial ability to pursue new energy studies on its own, so it depends on federal partnership funding rather than any in-house generation-technology roadmap. A separate web listing suggests QEC is formally named as a participant in Canada's SMR Action Plan in a research-only, wait-and-see capacity, but the source page could not be fetched (repeated certificate errors), so that specific claim is reported here only as an unverified lead, not a finding.

findings.question: What does a ton of fabricated TRISO cost, and which vendor's allocation covers its unit count?
findings.finding: DOE's HALEU Availability Program publishes only an aggregate delivery schedule, never a per-recipient breakdown. Its HALEU Allocation Process document commits DOE to 'seek to make available 21 metric tons ("MT") of HALEU' on a schedule of '3 MT by September 30, 2024, 8 MT by December 31, 2025, and 10 MT by June 30, 2026.' DOE's first round of conditional commitments (five of the 15 companies that applied: TRISO-X, Kairos Power, Radiant, Westinghouse and TerraPower) disclosed no kilogram figures, and neither did the third round, announced July 23, 2026, which added NASA and a second allocation to Radiant Industries. GAO's August 2026 report on federal uranium supply (GAO-26-107385) explains why no vendor-to-unit-count mapping exists: it found HALEU 'demands for commercial reactors remain highly uncertain' and separately flagged 'a potential future demand stream for unobligated HALEU to be used as fuel for microreactors under development' for the Department of Defense as still unquantified. No fetched source ties any recipient's kilogram allocation to its planned reactor unit count.
